blocks.text: DR JOHN GIBBS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Dr Gibbs, as always, could you begin by stating your full name for the recording, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr John Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: For your information and to remind us all of the evidential context of the evidence that you have been invited to give this morning, last week, when we were focusing upon the evidence in relation to the baby [Baby O] or [Baby O], the jury heard part of a witness statement that you made on 10 September 2018.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Part of that statement was read to the jury, which in terms informed the jury that you were the on-call consultant for the evening night shift of 23 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that as part of your duties on that evening, you attended at the neonatal unit to discover that [Baby O] was extremely ill and receiving cardiorespiratory resuscitation directed by your colleagues, Drs [Dr B] and Brearey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that was in progress when I arrived on the unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that you had some, in your words, peripheral involvement in the resuscitation that was already underway and was being led by Drs [Dr B] and Brearey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And in the circumstances, you deemed that your skills and time were best served directed towards [Baby O]'s triplet siblings, [Baby P] and [Baby R]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, because many of my colleagues were already helping [Baby O]. But I remember feeling uncomfortable when I arrived on the unit and saw [Baby O] and I thought, "Oh no, not another one", because I had become increasingly concerned, and I know that my consultant colleagues shared this concern, but I'd been increasingly concerned at the accumulating number of unusual, unexpected, inexplicable deaths and collapses that had been happening on the neonatal unit, and the fact that Staff Nurse Letby had been involved in all of them.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What did you do with your time immediately after moving away from [Baby O]'s cot side?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sadly, it was apparent that the resuscitation was not proving successful in [Baby O], and at the time I assessed [Baby P], [Baby O] had just died. So then I turned my attention to [Baby P] and his brother, [Baby R].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm grateful. If we could go, with Mr Murphy's assistance, to our tile 134, which is an event timed at 18.00 hours, on 23 June. If we could go to the underlying material, please, Mr Murphy. We will see a note made by your junior colleague, Dr Cooke, which records a review undertaken by you in her presence; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What was the purpose of that review?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To assess [Baby P] -- given that his brother had just died, to assess his state of health.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Whilst we are, of course, focusing upon [Baby P] for obvious reasons here this morning, did you, at or about the same time, conduct an identical review of his surviving triplet brother, [Baby R]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I did. It was [Baby P] first and then [Baby R] afterwards.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What did you discover upon examination of [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That he appeared very well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you expand upon that, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. As Dr Cooke has written down there, at the top she is saying his temperature is fine, 36.6. SVIA is spontaneously ventilating in air, he was breathing in air. He was tolerating his nasogastric milk feeds he was receiving, with a normal respiratory rate and heart rate recorded there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The OE is examination -- the on examination findings. [Baby P] was active when he was examined, the CR is capillary refill, less than 2 seconds, that is indication of normal circulation. He had a normal respiratory pattern, his breath sounds were clear and his abdomen -- that means his chest was clear.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Abdomen full and mildly distended, but there was no tenderness on palpating his abdomen, there were no masses to feel and his bowel sounds were active.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, one finding was that there was mild erythema, reddening or redness, at the base of his umbilicus. At this stage little [Baby P] was just 3 days old, he still had an umbilical stump from where his umbilical cord had been cut, and there was a plastic peg, a plastic clip around the umbilical stump, and it was likely he had a nappy on that was undone to examine his tummy. It's likely that that clip had been rubbing against his tummy and that's why there was a bit of redness there. So Dr Cooke, to be sure there was nothing wrong with the umbilicus, had said there was no swelling nor exudate -- that's on the umbilicus. The femoral pulses were present and heart sounds were normal.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that was a normal examination apart from the mild reddening below the umbilicus.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And to give context tot that normal examination, [Baby P] was by now in his third day of life?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And the clinical backdrop in the days from birth to 18.00 hours on 23 June, were you -- did you satisfy yourself that all appeared well between birth and this juncture?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, remarkably well for a triplet. Very well grown for a triplet. He'd needed a little help with his breathing with CPAP for the first 24 hours, for the next 12 hours the Optiflow, and then for the 12 hours before I saw him on this evening he had needed no help with his breathing at all and he was tolerating
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: his milk feeds so he was making very good progress, very good weight, excellent for a triplet baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm grateful. So having identified a single issue of potential concern, that being the umbilicus -- in or around the umbilicus, I should say -- what did you plan in relation to that potential issue?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, the plan was modified for [Baby P] to be more cautious than usual given the fact his triplet sibling had just died. So for another baby I would not necessarily have undertaken all these investigations, nor started any additional treatment, but given that [Baby O] had just died, we decided for [Baby P] -- I decided for [Baby P] to do a number of blood tests to look for any possible infections, that's the full blood count, the CRP, the protein that goes high with an infection, to take blood cultures, and a bilirubin level.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then the second part of the plan was, having taken those bloods, to start antibiotics. Now, [Baby P] had been on antibiotics for the first 36 hours of life because he had some breathing difficulties when he was first born. That rapidly settled and those antibiotics had been stopped. But I decided now to start, even without getting the results of the blood cultures and so on, which take a couple of days to show whether there's infection, to actually start antibiotics, a broad range antibiotic, a wide-ranging antibiotic called cefotaxime.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The flucloxacillin is particularly for skin infections, for example if you've got an infection in the umbilical stump spreading on to the skin, although I thought it was probably just rubbing of the umbilical clamp that had caused the redness.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But if one sibling has suddenly died, a possible cause of sudden death is overwhelming infection and so we're just being extra cautious with [Baby P], and the same later for his brother [Baby R], to cover them for possible infections even though he looked entirely well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So we started antibiotics on him and decided to do an abdominal X-ray.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Taking those in turn, firstly beginning with the taking of the blood and consideration of that sample, could we go, please, Mr Murphy, to tile 145, timed at 18.35. It is in our presentation as the obtaining of the sample, but does this tell us a little more about that sample?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is the blood culture, sample. So blood that was taken to look for any infection in the blood at that time. And
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: that just tells us -- this isn't the result, it's just telling us it was taken.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we scroll down, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. This is a result from that blood culture. It says at the very top there, underneath [Baby P]'s name and the fact he's a male boy, "Specimen collected on 23/6", at just after 18.30 in the evening. And I'm not quite sure what the recording on the 24th is, but that was in the -- that's the laboratory bit of detail there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then the result was authorised 6 days later, on the 29th, by the microbiologists and it's basically showing there was no growth of any bacteria after 5 days. So in retrospect, this shows that on this blood test there was no evidence of infection in [Baby P] from the evening of the 23rd June.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm grateful. There's more than one set of blood test results on our presentation, so let's deal with them now at tile 181, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this would seem to be -- it says Monday, 22 May 2017. That must have been an administrative process which is results of an analysis of a sample collected on 23 June 2016, received at the laboratory at 20.33. Could you tell us something about those results please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. Well, in relation to infection, we're looking to see whether the white blood count was abnormally high, suggesting a possible infection. And the first result there, white blood count, 6.9, and you can see if you look over to the right-hand column, that's well within the normal range of between 4 and 11. So a normal white cell count.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The other blood counts there, the platelet count was normal, the haemoglobin was normal. Those are not so important in relation to infection. In this blood test it's the white cell count that's most important.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we go down a little to towards the bottom four up from the bottom the "neuts" is the neutrophil count and the "lymps" are the lymphocyte count. Those are the two main kinds of white blood cells that are often raised in infection and both those results, 3.6 for neutrophils, 2.1 for lymphocytes -- sorry, the 3.6 for neutrophils is normal, the 2.1 for lymphocytes is a little low, but we're looking for abnormally high while cell counts suggestive of infection and that's not seen in this result for [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Putting those various component parts together, what was the inference that would be drawn from these results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: These blood tests do not suggest there was any infection in [Baby P] at the time they were taken, which is consistent with the clinical findings on examining him. There's a CRP level as well. I don't know if we're going to be looking at that. The CRP, which is a protein that goes high with infection, was also normal, again suggesting there was no infection with [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, could we go to the next tile, please, 182.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There it is at the bottom, the CRP result less than 1.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: A high level would be over 10 and usually well over 10 in an infection, but the CRP is not elevated in [Baby P], so a further indication there's no infection at that time it was taken.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just to provide context for this, we can see this was another sample collected on this date, 23 June, received at 20.33, and was ordered by Dr Cooke, who we know had been accompanying you at the 18.00 hours examination when this plan was formulated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So, please, putting the component parts of this septic screen together, what's the fundamental inference to be drawn from this data?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That there's no indication of infection, consistent with the clinical examination of [Baby P], so he was a well baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Another aspect of your plan was the ordering of an abdominal X-ray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we go, please, to tile 173. This is an X-ray, the radiograph for which is timed at 20.09 hours on 23 June.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could scroll down to look at Dr Wright's analysis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you, Mr Murphy. What did the radiograph show?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It just showed that there was a fair amount of gas/air in [Baby P]'s bowel all the way down his bowel. I mentioned that -it had been mentioned that during examination, his abdomen was mildly distended, that would be consistent with some air being in his bowel, seen on the X-ray. There were no other features to suggest any other more worrying bowel disorder like the
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: necrotising enterocolitis that was been discussed with other babies previously. He didn't show any signs of that on his Xray, he didn't show any signs of that on being examined either.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Some babies do swallow a fair amount of air, but we know in [Baby P] for the first 24 hours of life he'd had air under pressure blown in his nose with a CPAP device and for the next 12 hours he'd had a similar support from an Optiflow device, but that had stopped 12 hours before I saw him. It is likely, and I would have assumed, that the air in his bowel, being a little more than you would usually expect to see in a baby, was due to the treatment he'd had to support his breathing in the first 2 days of life. CPAP belly I think it's been called in the court before.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It has. Dr Gibbs, you told us that this formed part of your plan because of the reddening around the umbilicus and we can see, as an indication, the reason why the X-ray was ordered:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Mild abdo distension and peri-umbilical flare."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was there anything within the radiograph that were signs consistent with infection or inflammation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you have any further direct involvement in the care or treatment of [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you discover that his condition suddenly deteriorated on 24 June, leading to his death?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was extremely concerned to learn that later on, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I would not have expected that at all.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you remain there and answer any questions asked of you, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Gibbs, you made a statement to the police, didn't you, at the start of your part in this investigation, on 20 November 2017?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The copy I have goes to 41 pages and 123 paragraphs; does that sound about right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Was this on [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No, this is a general statement.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Oh, this wasn't [Baby P]'s statement?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No, not specifically [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have made so many statements to the police. I did make one that was quite long that included about seven babies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's right and it's general matters. You concluded that statement -- I'll tell you what you concluded the statement with. This is the statement made on 20 November 2017. Paragraph 123, page 130 of our statements:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "As of 20 November 2017 I have not noticed any medical or nursing member of staff involved in caring for infants on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital behaving inappropriately or providing improper care with respect to the infants discussed. Had I done so, I would have reported the behaviour to the appropriate nursing or medical line manager."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's how you conclude that, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. And also, had you got concerns about any member of staff and their adverse effect on the health of babies on the unit, you would have reported that to appropriate nursing or medical line managers, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think I said if I'd seen anyone doing something inappropriate, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm asking you if you had concerns about someone behaving inappropriately, that is something you would report to the appropriate nursing or medical line manager, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You began your evidence this morning by saying that you had become increasingly concerned about Nurse Letby's involvement in all of these events.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In fact, you had no concerns with regard to Nurse Letby until after the time of [Babies O & P]; that's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The death of the two of the [Surname of Babies O, P & R] triplets was the tipping point for realising something very abnormal and wrong was happening on our neonatal unit, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Before that point, had either Dr Brearey or Dr Jayaram shared any concerns with you about Nurse Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We discuss all the babies on the unit as outcomes. So every death, every collapse of a baby had been discussed, and Nurse Letby's involvement in some of the unusual or unexpected collapses had been noted, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: By involvement, in fact, that extends to presence on the unit at the time, doesn't it, as it happens?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Usually presence on the unit but most often caring for the baby concerned.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We have the babies we're dealing with here and we will see the evidence on that, Dr Gibbs. What I'm interested in knowing is your state of mind at the time you were dealing with [Babies O & P] given your comment about being increasingly concerned. Is this the situation, that by the time we get to [Babies O & P], Drs Jayaram and Brearey had identified the presence of Nurse Letby on various occasions that you had considered in your debriefs?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We all had, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You all had?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We'd all been involved in different babies, different consultants with different babies, as would have been -- as should be apparent now to the court. And we had noticed different members of staff, but there was a common factor and it had become clear to all of us involved in the babies that are being discussed in court.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You had actually reported no concern to the appropriate nursing or medical line manager at the time of [Babies O & P], had you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I said that I'd report if I saw someone doing anything that was abnormal or potentially harmful. I hadn't seen any member of staff do anything.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, and then I asked you; if you had concerns about any member of staff, would you report that to an appropriate nursing or medical line manager, and you said you would.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You just said that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But I knew it had been reported to the nursing manager on the unit, it had been reported to senior nursing managers in the hospital. Dr Brearey was our neonatal lead and Dr Brearey went to all the meetings reviewing the babies' deaths, so I knew it had been reported.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If you had genuine suspicion, Dr Gibbs, you, you would have acted, wouldn't you? You would have done?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We consultants all work together and I knew our lead for the neonatal unit had reported this.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You see yourselves as a team?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you still see yourselves as a team?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Working together with common interests?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, we do -- well, in every unit the doctors working on the unit work together as a team with the doctors and nurses yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We have seen how you had things to say that you wanted to say about Nurse Letby and this case in the course of these proceedings, Dr Gibbs, so I'm going to put to you again: if you had a concern, a genuine concern, you would have wasted no time in saying plenty about it at the time it arose to the managers?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, maybe I should qualify what I said at the end of that 41-page statement, that I would have reported it: I would have ensured it had been reported. I knew it had been reported.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The reality is, as we stand here now and as you talk about these events, you are now heavily influenced by a bias against Nurse Letby that applies to all of you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was most heavily influenced by what was happening to the babies on the unit. It wasn't scrutinising Nurse Letby's involvement, it was noticing -- and I have discussed this when I have given evidence before -- the unusual nature, the unexpected
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: nature or the inexplicable nature of the deaths and collapses that had been discussed. That was what was noticed first.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then it was realised what was the common factor in all of these and there was only one common factor.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you raised no concern whatsoever, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We had discussed this concern amongst ourselves and, yes, I had raised this concern with my fellow consultant paediatricians, and I knew that Dr Brearey had raised it with managers in the hospital.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And if you had genuine concerns and felt nothing was happening, you were perfectly capable of pursuing those concerns yourself, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You are capable of that, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but we work as a team.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Have you seen much of your team members in the course of this trial?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have seen some team members. We were waiting in the witness room. I haven't seen all of them.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Who have you seen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What, all the witnesses that have been waiting in the witness room over the 6 months I've been coming? This is the ninth, tenth patient I've given evidence on.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Consultants I'm asking about, Dr Gibbs, consultants.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Dr B] was here yesterday when I was waiting to give evidence. I saw [Dr C] some months ago. Dr Brearey I saw a few weeks ago and he's in the witness waiting room today. I've seen -- oh, eight, nine, ten of the nursing staff. And I saw Dr Jayaram a few months ago.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And have you been in touch with Dr Brearey or Dr Jayaram or [Dr B] about what's happened in this trial whilst it's been ongoing but outside court?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, we've been told not to talk about it. No, we haven't talked about the evidence that we are giving at all. It has been extremely difficult because we work as a team and ever since these concerns first arose 6 to 7 years ago, we've been
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: constrained in discussing it openly with the nurses, and even amongst us doctors, particularly after the police got involved. So it has been difficult but, no, I've not discussed the evidence I've given nor the evidence my colleagues have given whilst this trial has been running.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And have you followed the course of the trial on the newspaper reports there have been?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't help seeing some of the newspaper reports. The local paper, the Chester Chronicle, that I get each week and I have always read for the 28 years I've been in Chester runs front page reports on it.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Mm. And have you followed any kind of social media or do you not follow social media at all?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't follow social media, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If you -- have you at any point in the course of this investigation discussed -- I'm not going to ask what they are -your views on what has happened with your consultant colleagues?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Seriously?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. What, during the trial?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No, during the investigation. Let me be clear.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Oh, the investigation? Before the trial began?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Before the trial.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, we discuss every baby who dies on the unit or has an adverse event, like a collapse. That was discussed 6 or 7 years ago for every baby and we discussed it then in the 11 months before the police got involved after we raised concerns following [Baby P] and [Baby O]'s deaths.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In the 11 months when senior managers were extremely resistant to involving the police, we had to discuss what had happened because we had to keep insisting that the police ought to be involved.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But in fact, at no point during the time these events were taking place did any of you contact the police, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, that's difficult. As I've said, Nurse Letby seemed to be involved in all the cases that concerned me. I have only
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: been involved in some of them. My other consultants were involved in other babies. None of us, regrettably, realised that two babies had been poisoned with insulin, so we did not have the full picture. So it's uncertain at what stage we should have gone to the police.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But you're right, if we think someone is harming babies on the unit, it is our duty to take action to ensure the safety of the babies and that was done.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The disagreement, Dr Gibbs, may be less than you think.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not suggesting there is not some degree of suspicion at the relevant time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What I'm raising is simply that nothing was done at the time because that is all that it was at that point: there was a suspicion, there was a finger-pointing that was going on, just based on her presence on the unit at the time of events taking place. That's as far as it went.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At the time of events that I had never seen in my career before, that were unusual and unexpected, as I keep saying, it was those events that worried us most.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's what raised the concern. Then in medicine, it's not an exact science, you cannot always explain everything, which is highly unsatisfactory. So yes, just occasionally a patient dies and, despite extensive investigations and even a post-mortem, you cannot be sure what's happened. But this was happening again and again on our unit over that year and that cannot be just coincidence or just bad luck, there must be a cause.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that's when we began to realise who was involved with these babies, looking at each nurse, each doctor, and then there was one common cause that was identified, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Well, I'm not going to repeat the territory that I've covered already. Thank you, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR DRIVER
Simply on the subject of reporting, was there at the time within the Countess of Chester Hospital an established protocol for the reporting of issues of fundamental concern?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, there was a system called clinical incident reporting, but that's when you've seen something wrong or some mishap has happened. But as I've said, I did not see any member
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: of staff ever do anything wrong to a baby that should have been reported, otherwise that would have been reported. But I had reported a number of clinical incidents, you know, over that year.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I can't remember which ones they were and I'd have to re-look at records I don't have ready access to now I'm retired.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The reporting system that you have just referred to, which is typically used for the reporting of mishaps, to use your phrase, is that sometimes called the Datix system?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. That's clinical reporting or the Datix system.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you deem that an appropriate medium for the reporting of fundamental concerns, the likes of which you've shared with the jury this morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, because that is a system we report an incident when it's happened at the time. The concern that I have described this morning, that was building up by the time [Babies O & P] were on our neonatal unit, had built up over a series of time. It wasn't one particular incident, it was unusual and unexpected incidents keep on happening and clinical incident reporting wouldn't have picked that up, it's a trend over time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As to the communication of the consultant team's concern, joint concern, to the management, is there a chain of command, as it were? Is there an appropriate or designated consultant whose responsibility it was to communicate on behalf of the team?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Any of us consultants, and indeed any nurse, any member of staff, can report concerns, but there is a standard way that it's supposed to be done.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Brearey was our lead clinician for the neonatal unit -- I'd been the lead clinician for the neonatal unit some years earlier -- and, as part of his responsibilities, he regularly reviewed baby deaths and baby adverse outcomes with members of the risk management team in the hospital and with senior nurses from the ward. It was during those reviews and a copy -- a summary of those reviews were circulated to all of us consultants, that I knew the presence of Staff Nurse Letby had been raised several times by Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Turning briefly to the Datix system, if and when a clinician or a nurse reports an incident through that system, to whom does it go? Who would receive the notification?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It goes to the risk management team in the hospital, whose job is to look at risks within the hospital, to assess the severity and the impact of any adverse or mishap that -- adverse incident or mishap that's been reported. It comes back to each department for them to review it and that's where Dr Brearey, as lead clinician for neonatology, sat down with senior nurses to review it and then a summary of that comes round to us, to all of the consultants in the unit. From time to time senior people in the hospital, and I believe the person at the time that had overall responsibility for risk management was the director of nursing, but also for medical involvement it would be the medical director as well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I know -- I knew at that time that concerns had been raised by Dr Brearey with the most senior managers in the hospital relating to those Datix reviews, looking at the deaths of babies on the unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions for Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: No, I don't, thank you. There's one matter arising out of something that you said that I think will be clarified by subsequent evidence, but I won't ask you to give the answer. I think we'll find it from another source.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Is Dr Gibbs --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's very unlikely that Dr Gibbs will --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Can I add one thing about safety concerns and what we did about it?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: After the deaths of [Baby P] and [Baby O], and very regrettably too late, tragically late for them, because the concern, as I said, had reached a tipping point, safety measures were introduced and one of those key safety measures that we consultants insisted on was that Staff Nurse Letby was removed from the neonatal unit. And that wasn't a simple, straightforward decision because a month later senior managers met with us and wanted Staff Nurse Letby to come back to the unit and we said that should only happen if we had closed circuit television in each room on the unit. That was not -- the TV cameras didn't come, but neither did Staff Nurse Letby come back to the unit. And over the next 11 months before the police were called in, we had to resolutely resist repeated attempts by management for Staff Nurse Letby to come back to the unit. So yes, if you had safety concerns, you ought to do something about it and that's what we as a group of consultants did.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can I confirm two things, my Lord, if I may?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And if you were really concerned you could have asked for CCTV before then, couldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- as a member of staff is entitled to if they feel they've been treated badly?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have no further questions.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right.

blocks.text: -- until it is over? Thank you very much indeed.

Your answers to the questions re pneumothorax, would you be better placed to expand upon those answers if you considered the X-rays that were referred to?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, could you please put up tile 574? An X-ray timed at 15.36. It's the radiograph. If we go down to the radiologist's analysis. You haven't --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go down to the X-ray with the pneumothorax in it before the chest drain is inserted, that would be helpful, please.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Of course. One moment. Could we go to tile T400, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's worth -- I don't know what's been obviously discussed before, but there's two forms of pneumothorax that we can consider for neonates. And this is something we'd call a simple pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: As opposed to?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: A tension pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So a tension pneumothorax is a clear cause for sudden collapse in babies. And a pneumothorax is where there's a leak of the gas between the alveoli in the lung and the lining of the lung and that gas escapes and fills the gap between the lung and the chest wall. That's the simple pneumothorax that you can see on the screen in front of you today.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: In some cases the gas continues to fill that space between the lung and the chest wall, so at a certain point it becomes under pressure and moves the central portion of the chest, which is
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: the heart and the great vessels, over to the other side of the chest, and in doing so, under that tension, causes obstruction to blood vessels, airways and things like that, and can cause sudden collapse.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency, which needs depressurising -- the tension that's built up, which is the life-saving manoeuvre before you insert a chest drain. So there is no evidence of tension pneumothorax on that X-ray. It looks like a simple pneumothorax and I can tell that because -- can I use the cursor?
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Do you want to move the image or just point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you can see the trachea here following on from the endotracheal tube (indicating). The dark area here (indicating) is the trachea following along there.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That's the make(?) out of the trachea. And somewhere down here (indicating) it branches left and right in this direction. So that is following the normal course and you can see that this area here (indicating) is called the mediastinum in the central part of the chest and this area here (indicating) is the shadow for the heart. That's what in what we would call normal position in the chest so there's no shift in the mediastinum, no shift in the heart and no shift in the trachea. So this baby has a simple pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So the left lung is fully expanded and the right lung is partially expanded, so I wouldn't expect anything other than perhaps a mild degree of oxygen requirement and maybe a slight increase in respiratory rate, but certainly nothing that would cause a collapse of this baby. This baby doesn't have a tension pneumothorax and I wouldn't expect, looking at this X-ray, this to be the cause for the collapse of [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Moving to another radiograph behind our tile 434. This was a portable machine at around, we think, 12.30 as best we can time it from the clinical notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There's a chest drain in situ, you can see going in on the right. The simple pneumothorax has resolved, the lungs have re-expanded on to the chest wall, and again the heart and the mediastinum are in the correct position.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Would you care to read the radiologist's analysis or are you content with your own analysis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I am content it shows the resolution of the right-sided simple pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The final X-ray being the one that I first took your attention to. For the sake of completeness, can we go to that at our tile 574?

blocks.text: As mentioned earlier, this one, timed by the equipment at 15.36.53, what do you see there?

blocks.text: Again, a fully expanded left and right lung. Heart and mediastinum in the normal position. A different sort of chest drain in this time, which is called a pigtail catheter drain, which is inserted in a different way to the drain that you could see earlier. A similarly expanded chest wall.

blocks.text: You were asked questions by my learned friend as to whether you had considered whether the pneumothorax may have contributed to [Baby P]'s deterioration. I paraphrase.

blocks.text: Having reminded yourself of the X-rays, would you like to --

blocks.text: It's more likely that the pneumothorax developed as a result of being ventilated rather than a cause for any sudden deterioration off or on a ventilator. And clearly, it was identified and it was managed appropriately in terms of putting a chest drain in.

blocks.text: To paraphrase that, more likely a consequence of the response to the collapse as opposed to the cause of the collapses plural?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: A consequence of the treatment for the collapse and it seemed to be managed appropriately, yes. It's recognised as a common complication for mechanical ventilation.

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.

blocks.text: Do you recall whether there were any issues in that regard when it came to [Baby P] at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't recall any issues with that.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Despite that good chest movement and air entry, was there any spontaneous respiratory effort from [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, there was no breathing effort from [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: You describe his perfusion as poor; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: And that you observed his heart rate in fact had fallen gradually over the next 1 to 2 minutes after the initial collapse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, correct.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: And it was, as you've told us, when his heart rate dropped below 60 beats a minute, that's when chest compressions were started?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: We've heard that the resuscitation process is a process with set drugs, set intervals, and recognised practices and procedures; is that a fair summary?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's true.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Who administered the resuscitation to [Baby P] that afternoon when you were there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That would have been the team from the Countess of Chester together with me and I would assume that the nurse who was doing the transfer with me as well, although I'm not sure how much of that I've written down, so I can't be sure. That would be standard practice.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: During the course of that resuscitation, did [Baby P] receive multiple doses of adrenaline and sodium bicarbonate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He did, yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Do your records indicate that, during that interval between 15.15 and 15.54, he received seven doses of adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: I think three doses of sodium bicarbonate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: A dose of phenobarbitone?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Just explain that drug to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Phenobarbitone is a drug to treat fits or seizures and that was given as we had no explanation for why [Baby P]'s condition had changed and on the small chance that this was actually being caused by a seizure or a fit, he was given this medicine. It had no effect.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: You were there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: We've heard of your qualifications and experience. Was there anything that you could see as these events were unfolding as to any other possible cause for this collapse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We didn't think it was a seizure, it was just that it's one treatable cause for a baby who deteriorates. And there was no obvious cause, it didn't fit with any obvious reason for [Baby P] to have deteriorated from the condition he was in before.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: You have noted he received a fluid bolus and a dose of atropine in addition.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Atropine, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Atropine is given in babies who have a slow heart rate as it has an effect on the nerves that control the heart's regular beating rhythm and can speed it up in certain situations.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Were you satisfied that the intravenous lines were working well at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, they were working well throughout.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: And was [Baby P] continually reassessed throughout the resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He was continually monitored and being reassessed by the team throughout.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Bearing in mind what you told us about the lack of obvious cause for what was going on, were there conversations ongoing between everybody present?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The conversations were going on throughout the resuscitation as to what might have caused this collapse and whether any other different treatment should be -- could be administered.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: You mentioned airway and breathing or certainly airway and air entry at the start of the resuscitation. Did anything change with the ventilation and the air entry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did they deteriorate or remain good?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They remained good. There was no problem with the airway.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Were you satisfied that, in those circumstances, air entry was perfectly good?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Was there an intermittent and audible heartbeat?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Intermittently there was a heat beat audible, yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: And what about any ECG trace, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There was intermittently a slow and irregular heart trace.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Okay. You've described and confirmed earlier that this resuscitation went on between 3.15 and 3.54, so 39 minutes according to that note. Did there come a point during this prolonged resuscitation when you felt you had to speak to [Baby P]'s parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right. I think I've recorded that I spoke to [Dr B], discussing that we ought to speak to [Baby P]'s parents to discuss the futility of any further resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Okay. And was resuscitation in fact stopped at approximately 4 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: During the course of those conversations that you've told us about, did anyone successfully identify the cause of this collapse or --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, there was no cause identified and we did not have a reason to explain the collapse.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: After [Baby P]'s passing, did a debrief take place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Where did that take place, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It took place in a small room that formed part of the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Do you happen to recall who was present at the debrief?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't recall, other than [Dr A], who I've mentioned in the statement. I don't recall who else was in the debrief but it would have been the team. The purpose of the debrief is to make sure there was nothing that we think we've missed, but in
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: particular to look after the well-being of the staff involved in it.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Any conclusions reached as a result of that debrief?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There were no conclusions as to any of the clinical questions as to what had happened to [Baby P]. But just that we felt we had carried out the resuscitation well and in accordance with all the appropriate guidelines.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Other than participating in that debrief, did you have any further dealings with [Baby P] after that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I didn't, no.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Were you informed by [Dr B] that she would be informing the coroner?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: And that a post-mortem would be discussed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Before you left Chester, did you have then cause to discuss the situation with [Baby R]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Were you invited to transfer [Baby R] to the bed that was now available at Liverpool?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct. We had two unexplained deaths and given that we didn't know why that had happened, we felt it was most sensible to observe him in an intensive care unit.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Did you examine [Baby R] at that stage of the day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Do you remember roughly what time this would have been?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't recall, I think the time's in my statement.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Did you find that [Baby R] was on high flow humidified oxygen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Did you find him to be stable?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Was he pink and well perfused?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Alert and active with normal tone?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Did you find that his chest was clear but there was minimal recession?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: I think you described that as a mark of increased effort of breathing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: But common to premature babies?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Common to premature babies and the reason he would be receiving the high flow.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: His saturations were at 100%?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: He had no heart murmur and his femoral pulses were good?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: You examined his abdomen, which was soft and not distended?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Bowel sounds were normal?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Taking all that into account, you reached the view that he was stable for transfer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: And that's what you then undertook?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: I think you've recorded that transfer was uneventful.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, uneventful.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: And on arrival at Liverpool, did you go through the same sort of process that we've heard, the handover to the staff that then take over the care of [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Sorry, [Baby R].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We would then handover to the Liverpool unit staff.
blocks.speaker: RACKHAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Dr Rackham, thank you, I have no more questions. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: milk on two separate occasions, he also had a desaturation into his 80s, in other words his oxygen saturation dropped to his 80s, and it should be over 90.

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What conclusions did you come to as to the causes of those events?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was at a loss to explain how this baby had collapsed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's be... I was concerned from the night before because of the failure to establish milk, et cetera.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But there was clearly a significant deterioration at 09.40. Whether that -- my opinion was that he was resuscitated appropriately but the chest X-ray at 11.57, I think, showed a pneumothorax. My opinion was that the pneumothorax had been caused by -- as a result of the resuscitation. In other words, if you do bag a baby, you exert high pressure into the lung and you can cause a lung leak.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So I thought the pneumothorax had been caused by the resuscitation, I did not think that the pneumothorax was the result of his collapse. And from what [Dr B] said yesterday, and I agree, the chest X-ray did not show a tension pneumothorax. In other words, there was an air leak there but there was no sign of tension pneumothorax, which is life-threatening and needs urgent intervention.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So they treated the pneumothorax properly and from there on, I really was, and still am, stuck as to why he had further collapses and his final resuscitation was unsuccessful.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The only thing I could think of was that he'd suffered complications from the pneumothorax. Now, what I mean by this is this: going back to the bad old days where my generation spent a lot of time putting chest drains into babies who had bad lungs, and from time to time, despite inflating the lung the baby would not recover. The reason they would not recover, almost certainly, was that the collapse would have contributed to a condition called pulmonary hypertension. And pulmonary hypertension interferes with blood flow to and from the heart. That makes the pulmonary hypertension worse, you get a vicious cycle.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore in the bad old days, despite treating pneumothoraces with chest drains, when you're dealing with bad lungs, I thought, oh, this may explain from a physiological point of view why he failed to recover.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You've presumably listened to the evidence that's been given to the jury over the last few days concerning [Baby P]'s course of collapses and treatment?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And in particular, to Dr Brearey, who told us about an echo?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The cardiac echo was normal. What he meant by that was that there was no sign of pulmonary hypertension. So that tends to reduce my conviction in relation to [Baby P]'s death being the result of complications of his pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The other point, of course, is that unlike the bad old days, [Baby P]'s lungs were pretty normal before his pneumothorax. You know, he was not requiring oxygen, chest X-ray looked pretty good. Therefore he would not, in my opinion, have been a high risk for pulmonary hypertension following a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What about the effect of the gas in his bowel?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. There was a lot of gas in his bowel from the X-ray of 8 pm the night before --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The 23rd, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- which I commented on. The radiology report, which I respect, said there's a lot of gas there, but did not comment on the fact that there was too much gas there or that the presence of this gas was abnormal. So I left it as something that, you know, well, the radiologists have reported on the presence of lots of gas, which I've queried.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Looking back on it, I wonder whether the excess gas, I'm talking now from 8 pm the night before, may not necessarily have been natural. The baby was not on CPAP and he was not on nasal prongs, Optiflow. So it begs the question whether excess gas in his abdomen at 8 pm the night before was the result of air being injected down his nasogastric tube some time before 8 pm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: 8.09 being the precise time.

blocks.text: Sorry, yes, 20.09. Now, if you've got loads of air in the intestine, it's going to bloat you. In other words, you know, your intestine is full of air. He hasn't started getting a good regular bowel action.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That could contribute to the fact that he was not absorbing his milk as one would expect of a well premature baby. So whilst in my reports 5 years ago and 6 years ago I thought we should look at events from the aspiration of milk, 14ml of milk, late on the 23rd, I think we should look further backwards to the time that the X-ray showed lots of gas in his abdomen.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, to be fair to you, if you look at paragraph 14 of your report of 24 March 2019, paragraph 14 of that report. It's your third report of 24 March 2019.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, where I say and I quote:
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "I remain suspicious of the large volume of air noted in the stomach and intestines found on X-ray."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then I go on:
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "It may be that the sequence of events was this..."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you then say in effect what you've just said.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Excess air in the stomach and intestine, splinted the diaphragm, this would have compromised his breathing", et cetera.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. In your opinion are there any credible natural causes for [Baby P]'s premature death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are none, really, because we've gone through them all. Infection/sepsis is top of most people's list.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There was no sepsis. There was no significant haemorrhage. He did not have necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: He had no brain problem. We know, because he has a surviving triplet who's an identical triplet, that there was no congenital issue. So [Baby P]'s collapse and death cannot be explained on the basis of a natural event if one accepts the opinion of the doctors who -- experienced doctors who looked after him that pulmonary hypertension as a complication of pneumothorax is not a sufficient explanation for his death.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Those are all the questions I had for you. Thank you, Dr Evans. I don't know whether...

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I believe you are, my Lord, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON
